extracted.intended_audience: members of the public (individuals, groups, experts, and SLTT governments) who want to submit comments on proposed federal regulations
extracted.subtask_short: writing public comments on federal rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and submitting effective public comments on U.S. federal agencies' proposed rules, including recommended comment structure, substantive evaluative criteria, audience-specific approaches, and the procedural mechanics for finding and filing comments (Federal Register and Regulations.gov).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction — explain interest and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: An introduction where you explain why you are interested in the regulation and highlight any experience with the subject of the rule that may distinguish your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State who you are and why you are commenting; highlight relevant lived experience, professional background, or organizational role that gives weight to your observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background — identify the relevant part of the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A background section where you clearly identify the relevant part of the regulation you are commenting on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific sections, regulatory text, CFR citations, RINs, or docket numbers so the agency can easily locate what you reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis — argument and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis that lays out your argument and evidence (including with clear citations to any helpful research)—for example, how the action impacts you and what you care about; whether the agency anticipated or estimated these impacts correctly; any unintended consequences of this approach that the agency did not consider; and what additional details from the agency would help you better understand the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain impacts concretely, point out errors or gaps in agency analysis, describe unintended consequences, and ask for clarifying information the agency omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — specific changes suggested
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations describing your suggestions to the agency and identifying specific changes you would advise—for example, providing a different way of addressing the problem the agency may not have considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer concrete, actionable alternatives (revised regulatory text, parameters, or methods) rather than only objecting; explain why your proposal better addresses the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion — recap arguments and recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion which recaps your main argument and lists your recommendations again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the key points and restate the most important recommended changes for clarity and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance — provide information directly relevant to analyzing the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective, relevant comments provide regulators with information to help them improve draft rules. Comments are typically most effective when they provide information directly relevant to analyzing the rule and its potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on facts, analysis, and perspectives that help the agency evaluate impacts and alternatives rather than only stating support or opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to agency prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay special attention to any prompts from the agency itself, such as questions or requests for data or evidence, within the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the agency's explicit questions because these highlight where the agency seeks information or is missing data; providing requested data is particularly useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evidence and cite sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis should include clear citations to any helpful research; provide data or point to public data sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite peer-reviewed studies, agency reports, datasets, or other credible sources; show how the evidence supports your position or undermines the agency's assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether the regulation addresses a real problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the problem that the regulation intends to address. Why is this regulation needed? What is the problem the agency is trying to address? Is it actually a problem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question the need for regulation or whether the proposed approach is proportionate to the problem; explain with evidence why the problem exists or does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs versus benefits analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the costs of the proposed regulation are justified by its benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide data or reasoned analysis about costs and benefits; challenge or support agency estimates where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional and non-monetizable impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider distributional analysis and costs or benefits that are hard to monetize. Those who bear the costs of a rule and those who enjoy its benefits are not always the same people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss who bears costs and who receives benefits, and address impacts that are qualitative (dignity, equity, fairness) when monetary valuation is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify missing perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the agency is missing a certain perspective. A proposed rule may have particular impacts on a specific group or community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how a perspective (e.g., small businesses, disability community, regional stakeholders) is absent from the agency's analysis and provide evidence or examples to fill that gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of lived experience (individual commenters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the most effective comments are from individuals who describe the impacts of a proposal in terms of their own lived experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe concrete 'on the ground' effects—how your behavior would change, specific incidents, or costs you personally incur—rather than only expressing a preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregated membership perspective (groups & associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups and associations can aggregate the concerns and experiences of their members to paint a broader picture of potential impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide aggregated data, member surveys, public data sources, or representative anecdotes; make both technical and value-based arguments on behalf of members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert/practitioner technical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical experts and practitioners can offer important insight into how the rule functions in practice, present helpful data, and provide expert analysis on alternate regulatory designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique the rigor of studies the agency relies on, suggest alternative sources or methodologies, and offer practicable technical recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: SLTT government perspective and scalability limits
rubrics_metrics.description: State, local, tribal, and territorial governments can provide helpful insight about local impacts, but agencies write rules for the entire country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide local data and context but note whether and how such data can be scaled to national analysis; recognize agencies may not use unscalable local data for primary estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight unintended impacts on other groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out unintended consequences where a proposal benefiting one group may harm another (accessibility tradeoffs, mobility issues, safety risks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples (as with tactile pavers) to show cross-group tradeoffs and suggest design or material alternatives to mitigate harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural step — locate documents and deadlines in the Federal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Federal Register to determine what agency regulations are out for public comment; the preamble identifies the date by which comments must be submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search federalregister.gov by keyword, RIN, or agency; read the preamble and 'DATES' section to find deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural step — submit via Regulations.gov using docket number
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov is the official site used to submit public comments for most notices and proposed rules. Use the docket number from the Federal Register document to find the docket on Regulations.gov and then click 'Comment'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can paste the docket number into Regulations.gov search, type your comment into the text box or upload a file; include the document/docket identifiers so the comment is attached correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal effect — agencies must consider and respond to significant, relevant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies consider comments the public submitted and, in publishing any final rule, must respond to relevant and significant comments; failure to adequately respond may be challenged in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make comments 'significant' and 'relevant' by providing evidence and reasoned analysis to increase the chance the agency addresses them in the final rule and to create a stronger record for potential judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasiveness is quality over quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of public comments submitted does not determine the outcome; particularly influential comments are often those that provide good reasoning and evidence or a perspective the agency had not previously considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reliance on volume; focus on well-reasoned, evidenced, and novel contributions rather than mass identical submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplicate/identical comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple identical comments are not likely to be more persuasive than if the comment had been sent only once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalize comments to include unique experiences or additional evidence rather than submitting verbatim copies of a template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point out flawed, inaccurate, or outdated agency information
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether proposed regulations are based on the best available scientific, technical, economic, experience-based, and other information. If you are aware of flawed, inaccurate, or out of date information the agency is using, explain that fact to the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific errors or outdated sources, provide corrected data or citations, and explain implications for the agency's analysis or proposed approach.
